metadata.geoclick:note: Shared style for every demo map, polygon (regions/states/provinces, built by build-map.ts) or point (towns/cities, built by build-points-map.ts) alike — one style serves both, see MAPS.md's 'Point-target design' section. The 'targets' source url is a placeholder (pmtiles://./tiles.pmtiles) — the map viewer composes the final style per map by replacing it with that map's own tiles.pmtiles URL. A polygon map's 'targets' source-layer has polygon features rendered by 'targets-fill'/'targets-outline'; a point map's has point features rendered by 'targets-circle' instead — each of the three is filtered by geometry-type, so only the matching pair ever renders anything for a given map's tileset (harmless no-op for the other). Polygon tilesets also have a 'labels' source-layer (one point per feature at its precomputed centroid) - not present for point maps, since a point target's own geometry already is its label anchor. Every tileset also has a 'lakes' source-layer (Natural Earth lake polygons within the map's overall bounding box, purely contextual — no hit-testing, no feature-state, just a lighter fill so a target whose border runs along a lake, e.g. Michigan on the Great Lakes, reads as a coastline rather than an unexplained gap next to its neighbors). A point map's tileset also has a 'context' source-layer (that country's admin-1 polygons from the same Natural Earth dataset build-map.ts uses for actual polygon targets, rendered by 'context-fill'/'context-outline' beneath the lakes/targets layers) — purely visual, no hit-testing, no feature-state: without it, a towns map's markers float with nothing showing the country's outline or internal admin-1 borders, unlike a polygon map where the targets themselves, filled edge to edge, already show the whole country. A polygon map's tileset has no 'context' source-layer, so these two layers are a harmless no-op for it, same pattern as 'targets-circle' being a no-op for a polygon map's tileset. This style deliberately does not render a name label layer: Geoclick is a place-recognition game, so showing region names on the map by default would give away the answer. The 'labels' source-layer still exists in the tiles for the app to use on demand (e.g. a per-click popup, a guided tour reveal, or a solved quiz target), just not as an always-on style layer or even a MapLibre symbol layer — a DOM-based maplibregl.Popup per solved/revealed target turned out more reliable than driving a symbol layer's opacity from feature-state, which hit MapLibre's collision/placement system hiding labels unpredictably even with text-allow-overlap+text-ignore-placement set (see QuizView.svelte). Since v0.6.0 (FT-23) the app collides those popups itself (app/src/lib/labelCollision.ts), so names never overlap - a label a more important name covers is hidden until the player zooms in. That keeps every name rendered by the browser, not by MapLibre, which is why the 'glyphs' URL at the top of this style is still unused and should stay that way: it points at a public font server, and the desktop and Android builds have to work with no network at all. promoteId 'name' lets the app call setFeatureState by target name directly (map.json's Target.name), without needing to query the source for a feature first — safe because target names are unique within a single map. Feature-states used across views: 'highlighted' (explore click, tour reveal), 'quizHover' (drag-to-match, region under the dragged slip), 'quizCorrect' (drag-to-match, region solved), 'quizRevealed' (drag-to-match, auto-solved after too many wrong attempts — distinct muted color, doesn't count as a real success), 'quizWrong' (drag-to-match, brief flash on whichever region was actually — wrongly — dropped on; takes priority over every other state since it's a transient overlay that can land on an already-solved region if a different slip gets dropped there by mistake). Base (non-interactive) fill/circle color is a categorical `match` on the 'colorIndex' feature-state (slots 0-5, six muted colours; an unset slot falls back to a neutral sand). Each target's slot is chosen at build time by graph colouring so no two adjacent targets share one - data/scripts/mapColors.ts writes it into map.json and geoclickMap.ts's createMap applies it as feature-state, so recolouring never needs a tile rebuild. The number of match arms must equal PALETTE_SIZE in mapColors.ts (mapColors.test.ts checks). The palette is kept away from the state colours - no green (quizCorrect), gold (quizRevealed) or red (quizWrong) - and quizHover is a deep blue, darker than the palette's light blue. fill-opacity/circle-opacity are also a `case` on the same feature-states: any named state (solved, hovered, wrong, revealed, explore-highlighted) renders at 0.85 fill / fully opaque circle, the unsolved default at 0.55 fill / 0.85 circle - high enough for the palette to read, low enough that solved stays distinct at a glance. See DECISIONS.md's 'Map colors' and 'Quiz solved-state contrast' entries. Since v0.8.0 (FT-33) there is a second, optional layer group this style deliberately does NOT declare: the Terrain layer (sea, rivers, named ranges and seas) lives in its own archive per map, terrain.pmtiles, and app/src/lib/terrainLayer.ts adds its source and three fill/line layers to the live map the first time the player presses the map bar's Terrain button. It cannot be declared here because MapLibre rejects a layer whose source is missing at style load, and the source must not exist until it is wanted - geoclickMap.ts pulls a whole archive into memory on the desktop and Android shells, which serve no range requests, so a layer that is off by default must not sit inside the tileset every map already loads. Its labels are DOM popups through labelCollision.ts at a negative priority, for the same no-glyph-server reason as every other name here.

A town's tap target, not its dot (FT-46). Invisible - circle-opacity 0 - and 22 px in radius against the dot's 9, so a finger gets about 44 px to hit, the floor the language picker and the zoom buttons already use (review F8). MapLibre hit-tests geometry rather than painted pixels, so a fully transparent layer still answers clicks and queryRenderedFeatures. Views bind their click to THIS layer instead of targets-circle, never both: this circle covers that one completely, so two bindings would fire two handlers for one tap and toggle a name straight back off. Last in the list, so it sits above the dot - it paints nothing, so that costs no appearance. No tile rebuild was needed: it is a style layer over a source that already exists.
